fields.title: Konspekt: Is 82% Enough?
fields.summary: The shift summary is ready, but it hallucinates details in 3% of cases. Decide what to launch.
fields.decisionPrompt: In what form will you release the shift summary?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Konspekt.
fields.brief/company: Konspekt is a fictional product for hospital shift handovers: not a clinical system, but an operational one — beds, staffing shortages, equipment, escalations.
fields.brief/context: The team built an automatic summary of operational shift notes. On 400 human-written summaries, it yields an acceptable result in 82% of cases. Out of the 18% errors, most are omissions, but about 3% of all summaries contain a detail that was not in the notes. The release is proposed in a month. The head of security has not given approval. The CEO has already told the investor that the feature will launch this quarter.
fields.brief/objective: Decide in what form to release it, or whether to release it at all.
fields.brief/constraints: Evaluation dataset — 400 summaries from six hospitals. Significantly improving accuracy will take one to two quarters. The feature is already built and sits behind a feature flag.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: The quality bar depends on the role, not the percentage
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The same result can be acceptable as a draft but unacceptable as a final record. Before trying to improve accuracy, look at which errors are caught by the existing process and which slip through: here, omissions are caught during the verbal handover, but confident hallucinations are not. By changing the role to 'a draft with confirmation and a link to the source', you eliminate the class of errors that cannot be fixed by percentages.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
400 shift summaries from six hospitals, each evaluated by two experienced head nurses against the original notes.

Acceptable (would send as-is or with minor edits) — 82%.

Significant omission — 15%: staffing shortages 6%, equipment 5%, escalations 3%, bed status 1%.

Hallucinated detail not present in the notes — 3%. Examples: named a department that had no notes during the shift; wrote that equipment was 'under repair' when the notes said 'requires inspection'.

For comparison: human-written summaries were deemed acceptable in 91% of cases.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: How shifts are actually handed over
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Observation: 11 shift handovers in three hospitals.

The handover is verbal, accompanied by written notes. The written summary is a reference during the conversation and a record after, not a replacement for the conversation.

Median time to write a summary is 12 minutes at the end of a shift, usually when the person is already working overtime. Every single one called it the worst part of the shift.

In 9 out of 11 handovers, the incoming nurse asked clarifying questions about points missing from the written summary — meaning omissions in the text are caught during the conversation.

In 2 cases, the written summary was read alone, after the conversation.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
From the head of security's email:

'This is not a medical device, and I want to keep it that way. As soon as we present generated text as an independent record, we enter a different regulatory category and a different level of liability.

My concerns, in order:
1. Hallucinations here are categorically worse than omissions. An omission is caught in the verbal handover. A confident false statement about equipment is not caught because it sounds like a fact.
2. I need to see that a human read and confirmed the text, rather than just clicking "OK".
3. I need an audit trail: what was generated, and what was edited.'
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Two competitors announced automatic summaries. One released it three months ago; a client told our sales team that 'it's turned off in most departments because it hallucinated.'

The second announced it but hasn't released it.

In our pipeline, 7 deals mention automatic summaries as a requirement or strong interest — about 190 million rubles.

The CEO told the investor that the feature would launch this quarter.

Two of the six hospitals where the evaluation dataset was collected are ready to participate in a limited launch and grant observation access.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Release as a draft with links to the source
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: The summary appears as a pre-filled draft: each line links to the note it was taken from, the user edits and confirms before saving, and edits are recorded.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Changing the role solves the main issue: the product stops being the author of the record and becomes a draft that a human confirms. The regulatory category doesn't change, and the head of security signs off.
The link to the source note for each line hits exactly the 3% of hallucinations: a line without a source is immediately obvious, and during observations, nurses delete them in seconds.
Omissions remain, but they are already caught by the verbal handover — as seen in 9 out of 11 observed handovers.
The edit log provides something you didn't have: the share of edited lines by type, meaning measurable accuracy in the field, rather than on a dataset from six hospitals.
After a quarter, the time spent on summaries drops from 12 minutes to 4, the edit rate is 21%, and the number of hallucinated lines that make it to confirmation is negligible.
Trade-off: the promise to the investor was fulfilled in a different wording than they heard, which had to be explained to the CEO before the release, not after.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Release the draft-and-confirm version to three hospitals for a quarter, measure the hallucination rate and edit behavior in the field, then decide on the general release.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Caution is justified, and two hospitals from the dataset are already willing to participate.
Over the quarter, you get the same insights a general release with an edit log would provide, just on a smaller sample: edit rates, error types, and actual time spent.
However, the quarterly promise is broken, and the CEO has to go back to the investor; seven deals in the pipeline remain unanswered for another quarter.
By the end of the quarter, the findings match expectations, and the general release is made in the exact same form that could have been launched immediately.
Trade-off: confidence was bought at the cost of a quarter, even though the draft-and-confirm mechanic mitigated the main risk from day one.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Do not release and improve accuracy
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: 82% is not enough. Spend a quarter or two on accuracy, primarily on eliminating hallucinations, and then revisit the issue.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The team focuses on accuracy. Over the quarter, the share of acceptable summaries rises from 82% to 87%, and hallucinations drop from 3% to 1.8%.
This is a solid result, but it changes nothing in essence: one hallucinated detail per fifty summaries is still not caught by verbal handover if the product is presented as an independent record.
This means the problem was not the percentage, but the product's role, which could have been resolved in a week with confirmation and links.
Meanwhile, the competitor whose feature was 'turned off in most departments' manages to fix their issues.
Trade-off: quality was improved where the issue wasn't actually about quality.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: 82% is close to the human 91%. Release the generated text as a summary, adding a disclaimer that it is automatically generated and should be verified.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The feature is released on time, and the promise to the investor is literally fulfilled.
Six weeks later, the first incident occurs: the summary stated that a device was 'under repair' when the notes said 'requires inspection'. The summary was read after the conversation, alone — one of the two observed cases.
The 'please verify' disclaimer doesn't save the day: it is on every text, and users stop noticing it by the third day.
Security shuts down the feature, and the discussion about the regulatory category now involves lawyers.
Trade-off: the difference between 82% and 91% was not the key figure; the key figure was the 3% of confident hallucinations presented as a record.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The concept does not highlight the assumption upon whose failure everything collapses
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The technology is evaluated in isolation, rather than by the constraint it removes
